cards.h: Most of the matter is missing
cards.b: The stars, gas and dust that we see, everything made of atoms, make up only about 5 percent of the universe's energy. About 27 percent is dark matter, which does not emit or absorb light but pulls with gravity. About 68 percent is dark energy. Dark matter outweighs ordinary matter by about 5 to 1.

Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky measured how fast galaxies move in the Coma Cluster. They moved so quickly that the cluster should fly apart unless it contained far more mass than the visible stars. He called the missing stuff dunkle Materie, dark matter. Few took it seriously.

In the 1970s Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured how fast stars and gas orbit in spiral galaxies, starting with Andromeda. If only visible matter existed, outer stars would orbit slower, as outer planets do. Instead the speeds stay flat out to the edges. Something invisible fills a huge halo around each galaxy.

Einstein's theory says mass bends light. A cluster of galaxies acts like a lens, distorting images of galaxies behind it. The amount of bending tells us the total mass, which is far larger than the visible stuff. In the Bullet Cluster (2006 analysis) two colliding clusters show the lensing mass lying separately from the hot gas, direct evidence that the mass is not ordinary gas.

The pattern of ripples in the cosmic microwave background and the growth of the cosmic web both need dark matter. Without it gravity could not pull matter into galaxies in 13.8 billion years. Ordinary matter alone would be too smooth.

It is not ordinary atoms, and not neutrinos (too light and fast). Candidates: WIMPs (weakly interacting massive particles), axions (very light particles), or primordial black holes. Large underground detectors (XENON, LUX-ZEPLIN) have found no clear WIMP signal. Another idea, MOND (Milgrom, 1983), modifies gravity instead, but struggles to explain clusters and the CMB.

Galaxy rotation, galaxy clusters, lensing, the CMB, and cosmic structure all agree on the same amount, a rare case where unrelated methods converge. That is why most astronomers accept dark matter, even though we do not know what it is.

• 'Dark matter is black holes or dust.' Ordinary dark objects are limited by other measurements.
  • 'Dark matter and dark energy are the same.' They are different: one clumps and attracts, the other drives acceleration.
  • 'Scientists invented it to save a theory.' It was forced by measurements, and tested many ways.

India has a history in deep-underground particle physics: in 1965 TIFR's detectors in the Kolar Gold Fields mine, 2 km deep, recorded the first atmospheric neutrinos. A proposed India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) in Tamil Nadu's Theni district has faced delays. Researchers at IUCAA and TIFR work on gravitational lensing and large-scale structure, and on simulations that include dark matter.

• Dark matter is about 27 percent of the universe and 85 percent of its matter.
  • Evidence: galaxy rotation curves, cluster speeds, lensing, CMB, structure growth.
  • It does not interact with light; its identity is unknown.
  • WIMPs, axions and modified gravity are candidate explanations.

Think about it: (1) Why do flat rotation curves need extra mass? (2) What kind of observation could rule out WIMPs?
